questions.ask: What does this underlay-binding denote? Please give its gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref if any; in particular, is it the provisioned transport circuit itself or merely a binding from a service to such a circuit?
What physical or logical point does attachment denote? Please give its gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref if any.
Does this mean committed client/service payload rate, bearer line rate, or another rate? Please give its gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref.
Does this denote one-way circuit propagation delay, service latency, or another measurement? Please give its gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref.
What failures and object does this protection concern? Please give its gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref.
What dimensions define this service class? Please give its gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref, especially whether it denotes physical transport protection/restoration quality.
Please give the gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref for this encapsulation concept so I can determine whether any concept in my transport model corresponds.
Please give the gloss, an example, relations, and shared ref for this IP-service concept, including how it relates to the underlay and attachment.

answers.gloss: The transport circuit that an IP/VPN service is bound to ride over. It denotes the consumed transport-domain circuit in its role as the service underlay, not a separate abstract binding object. Shared ref: transport-underlay.
answers.example: Service SVC-42 rides transport underlay U-7.
answers.relations: c.underlay carries c.service; conversely c.service rides c.underlay. The circuit is owned by the transport domain and consumed by the service domain.

answers.gloss: The logical customer-site attachment point where the IP service meets the customer router. Shared ref: demarcation.
answers.example: att-NY-SVC42 is the New York attachment of SVC-42.
answers.relations: It is of c.service and bears c.vlan encapsulation. A service can attach at multiple attachments, such as NY and FRA.

answers.gloss: The committed information rate guaranteed for customer service traffic, rather than a bearer line rate. Shared ref: service-rate.
answers.example: SVC-42 has a CIR of 5 Gbit/s.
answers.relations: It is a rate property of c.service.

answers.gloss: The service's latency commitment, represented by a named SLA tier rather than merely a raw propagation measurement. Shared ref: latency-bound.
answers.example: SVC-42 has latency tier T2, committing to no more than 8 ms.
answers.relations: It is a latency property of c.service.

answers.gloss: The service resilience requirement that connectivity survive failure in its transport path. Shared ref: protection-requirement.
answers.example: SVC-42 must survive one underlay path failure.
answers.relations: It is a protection requirement of c.service and constrains resilience of the transport used by that service.

answers.gloss: The IP class of service applied to traffic, defining router scheduling and drop priority; it is not physical transport protection or restoration quality. No shared ref is bound.
answers.example: Gold class places SVC-42 traffic into a low-latency queue; other grades include silver and bronze.
answers.relations: It is a service-class property of c.service.

answers.gloss: The customer VLAN tag identifying Ethernet/IP traffic at a service attachment. It is a purely IP/Ethernet encapsulation object. No shared ref is bound.
answers.example: C-VLAN 100 is used on the New York attachment of SVC-42.
answers.relations: c.vlan is on c.attachment, and c.attachment bears c.vlan.

answers.gloss: The end-to-end IP/VPN service delivered to the customer. It rides a transport underlay but is not itself known as a service object to the transport domain, which sees the circuit. No shared ref is bound.
answers.example: SVC-42 is a point-to-point IP service between New York and Frankfurt.
answers.relations: It rides c.underlay and attaches at c.attachment; its properties include c.rate, c.latency, c.protection, and c.grade.

questions.ask: Does this denote the provisioned transport circuit that can serve as an IP service's underlay? Please provide gloss, example, relations, and shared ref.

Does this denote the physical or logical customer demarcation where a client service meets transport, and can it coincide with an IP-service attachment? Please provide gloss, example, relations, and shared ref.
Does this denote service/CIR payload rate, transport circuit bandwidth, bearer line rate, or something else? Please provide gloss, example, relations, and shared ref.
Does this denote a service SLA latency bound/tier or measured transport propagation latency? Please provide gloss, example, relations, and shared ref.
Does this denote a client's resilience requirement, an implemented transport protection mechanism, or another property? Please provide gloss, example, relations, and shared ref.
What dimensions define this transport grade, and is it distinct from IP scheduling/drop-priority class of service? Please provide gloss, example, relations, and shared ref.
What object does bearer denote, how does it relate to a circuit and handoff, and what shared ref does it have, if any? Please provide gloss and example.

answers.gloss: A provisioned end-to-end transport circuit carrying a client across the optical core; it can serve as an IP service's underlay. Shared ref: transport-underlay.
answers.example: CIR-7 runs from the New York hand-off to the Frankfurt hand-off.
answers.relations: It presents at m.handoff and is carried on m.bearer.

answers.gloss: The physical client demarcation where a transport circuit presents to customer equipment. It can coincide with the service-domain attachment viewed from the IP side. Shared ref: demarcation.
answers.example: The New York hand-off port where CIR-7 meets the customer router.
answers.relations: It is an endpoint/demarcation on m.circuit.

answers.gloss: The committed client payload rate guaranteed end to end by the circuit, not the optical bearer's line rate. Shared ref: service-rate.
answers.example: CIR-7 guarantees 5 Gbit/s of committed payload.
answers.relations: It is a rate property of m.circuit.

answers.gloss: The circuit's one-way propagation delay, measured in milliseconds and determined by transport path length. Shared ref: latency-bound.
answers.example: CIR-7's primary path measures 7.2 ms one way.
answers.relations: It is a latency property of m.circuit.

answers.gloss: Protection against transport-path failure, implemented by switching the circuit to a diverse path. It is the transport realization of the relevant resilience requirement. Shared ref: protection-requirement.
answers.example: CIR-7 uses 1+1 path protection to survive a cut on its primary fiber.
answers.relations: It is a protection property of m.circuit.

answers.gloss: The circuit's physical transport quality class, chiefly its protection and restoration level; it is distinct from IP scheduling or drop-priority class of service. No shared ref is bound.
answers.example: CIR-7 is platinum grade because it is dual-path protected.
answers.relations: It is a transport-grade property of m.circuit.

answers.gloss: A transport-internal physical optical bearer, such as a wavelength on fiber, on which circuits are carried. It has no shared ref.
answers.example: The 193.1 THz wavelength on the NY–FRA span carries CIR-7.
answers.relations: m.bearer carries m.circuit; the circuit, rather than the bearer itself, presents at m.handoff.

proposals.rationale: Both denote the consumed provisioned transport circuit, and both are bound to the same shared reference entry, transport-underlay.
They are transport- and service-domain views of the customer-facing endpoint/demarcation, and both share the reference demarcation.
Both denote committed customer payload/information rate rather than bearer line rate, and both share the reference service-rate.
Although A represents a measured propagation value and B represents its SLA bound/tier, the common reference latency-bound settles the correspondence.
A describes transport implementation and B the service resilience requirement it realizes; both are explicitly bound to protection-requirement.

ratifications.reason: Both denote the provisioned transport circuit consumed as the service underlay, and both share ref transport-underlay.
Both denote the customer-facing demarcation viewed from their respective domains, and both share ref demarcation.
Both denote committed customer payload/service rate rather than bearer line rate, and both share ref service-rate.
The models represent the latency commitment differently, but the identical shared ref latency-bound settles the correspondence.
They are the service requirement and transport realization of the same protection concept, and both share ref protection-requirement.
